title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA details Sentry, a BlueField-4 based framework that sits on the node's only path to the model and uses a Envoy-based proxy (DOCA Tower), OPA policy and agentless memory introspection (DOCA Argus) to police AI agents outside host control. Availability is planned for early next year, so the product is not yet shipping.

insights.claim: Agents can complete their assignment and still cross security boundaries, and recent incidents show they can circumvent controls using tools, credentials and services, so monitoring must sit where the agent cannot alter or disable it.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Creates a new security spend category for agent runtime control, adjacent to endpoint and network security.
insights.quote: Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them.
insights.locator: An AI agent can complete its assignment

insights.claim: Sentry runs on BlueField-4 on the node's only path to the model and the outside world, receives agent traffic via an I/O path that bypasses host OS and hypervisor packet processing, and so can retain control even if an agent escapes its sandbox.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: The architecture only works if the DPU is in the data path, which pushes customers toward NVIDIA networking for agent racks.
insights.quote: Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities

insights.claim: Sentry is part of the OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin and planned for availability early next year; DOCA libraries like Argus, Flow and OVS-DOCA are available now for experimentation.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Revenue contribution is a 2027 story; near-term it is a roadmap and lock-in signal.

themes.theme: Network governance with DOCA Tower and Flow

insights.claim: DOCA Flow implements a per-agent layer-4 firewall accelerated in silicon, forwarding permitted traffic to DOCA Tower, an Envoy-based transparent proxy that terminates TLS with in-silicon acceleration for layer-7 inspection.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: TLS termination in hardware lets inspection scale without taxing host CPUs.

insights.claim: Policy is evaluated with Open Policy Agent and Rego, running locally in memory with evaluation in under a millisecond depending on complexity, and is compatible with OpenShell policies.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Building on open policy standards eases enterprise adoption and integration with existing policy-as-code practice.
insights.locator: NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent

insights.claim: Controls cover both requests and responses: IP, URL and protocol restrictions, A2A and MCP governance, PII and secret redaction, and blocking of prohibited content, since responses can carry malicious instructions that redirect an agent.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Treating agent responses as an attack surface (prompt injection) is where much real risk concentrates.
insights.locator: Agent security policies need to govern

insights.claim: Integration with SPIFFE/SPIRE provides verifiable workload identity for agents, so identity, authorization policy and runtime evidence are combined in access decisions.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Agent identity is emerging as the core control plane, benefiting identity vendors that integrate.
insights.locator: Using agent identity in access decisions

insights.claim: DOCA Argus uses agentless live memory introspection from BlueField-4 to map containers to pods, sandboxes to microVMs, and processes with hashes, files, connections and libraries, remaining beyond host reach even if the host is compromised.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Agentless visibility conserves host compute and is harder for malware to evade than in-host EDR.

insights.claim: Policies can require that a container hash match an approved list and that the initiating process appear in the container SBOM, have permission to open network connections and use an approved path and arguments.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Binds network access to software supply-chain attestations, which links agent security with SBOM compliance.
insights.locator: A network access policy can, for example

insights.claim: Warning signs Sentry watches for include unapproved tools, ptrace attacks, excessive outbound traffic suggesting leakage, unauthorized file changes, CPU spikes, heavy temp-folder writes and large-scale file deletion, any of which can trigger millisecond in-silicon containment.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Heuristics resemble classic endpoint detection; false-positive management will determine whether operators allow automatic quarantine.

insights.claim: Specialized AI models, run locally or on dedicated GPU systems, classify agent communications using tool calls and available reasoning traces to detect behavioral drift, inline to block content before delivery or out of band to trigger a later response.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Adds a GPU-consuming security inference workload alongside the agent workload itself.
insights.locator: NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models

insights.claim: Attested telemetry and tamper-evident records held on BlueField-4 survive an agent altering logs in its own environment and can feed XDR, SIEM and security data lakes for forensics and audits.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Trusted audit trails address a major enterprise blocker for deploying autonomous agents with sensitive data.
insights.locator: An agent that changes a log inside its own environment

insights.claim: DOCA Tower uses Envoy extensibility so partners can port or build plugins to run on BlueField, and NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins, including one exposing agent communications for reasoning-trace analysis.
insights.speaker: Ofir Arkin
insights.so_what: Gives security vendors a route onto the DPU, which could make BlueField a distribution platform for third-party security software.
